# Ucchaṅgajātaka (Ja 67)

**ID:** Ja 67
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Ucchaṅgajātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** Sons Fall in a Mother’s Lap
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja67
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Ucchaṅgajātaka* (Ja 67) is a canonical Jātaka tale framed at Jetavana, where the Buddha recounts the story of a rural woman (*jānapaditthī*) [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877]. In the narrative, three men—a woman's husband, son, and brother—are falsely arrested as bandits while ploughing a field at the edge of a forest in the kingdom of Kosala [Lamotte 1988; Fausböll 1877]. Imprisoned and facing royal judgment, the woman arrives weeping before the king, repeatedly pleading for their release and asking to be given a "protective covering" (*acchādana*) [Sarao & Long 2017; Lamotte 1988]. When the king offers her a cloak (*sātaka*), she clarifies her meaning; moved by her tears, the king decides to release only one of the prisoners and bids her choose [Sarao & Long 2017; Lamotte 1988]. The woman chooses to spare her brother over her husband and her son, reflecting that another husband or child might be obtained, whereas a brother cannot; impressed by her reasoning, the king pardons all three [Sarao & Long 2017; Cabezón 2017].

Scholars have drawn attention to the tale's literary and social motifs. Lamotte observes a striking concordance of narrative details between this Jātaka and a famous account in Herodotus [Lamotte 1988]. Cabezón highlights the episode as a clear statement in Buddhist storytelling where fraternal devotion is depicted as superseding both erotic attachment and parental love [Cabezón 2017]. Sarao and Long likewise discuss the story in connection with early Buddhist perspectives on marriage and female agency [Sarao & Long 2017].

SuttaCentral records translations into four languages, including an English translation by Bhikkhu Sujato [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus detects no cross-language parallels with score ≥ 10, but records four Pali-internal reuse passages shared with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (with its longest shared segment spanning §0.4–2.1 and §1948_4–1952_0) [DharmaNexus].
